title: Systems Programming and Machine Organization
subtitle: Dr. Charles Dorner
author: Dr. Charles Dorner
description: Learn systems through the same problem, mechanism, trace, UML, C++, and practice structure as Design Patterns. All 61 chapters include a complete demonstration, a boundary-tested extension lab, and explained answers.
provenance: All 61 supplied presentations and transcripts remain intact, with all 1775 slide records and existing study IDs. The added study curriculum supplies 61 original C++17 demonstrations, 61 lab starters, 61 reference solutions, exact source-linked diagram panels, six independent exercises per chapter, and 122 glossary entries. Models of hardware and OS behavior are labeled; they do not make real system calls. Original companion listings named by some supplied lectures were absent from the upload and are not claimed as tested here. The race-condition correction remains visible beside its source lesson.

glossary.definition: The inputs, results, and rules that callers and implementations agree to.
A part of a system that performs one kind of work through a defined boundary.
A parameter object initialized from the argument; this vector has independent element storage.
Another name for the caller’s object, with no new copy of that object.
A bit pattern selecting which bit positions an operation should affect.
A fixed group of bits used to store one value within a larger word.
Unsigned arithmetic reduces a result modulo one more than the type’s maximum value.
A rule that must hold before an operation can safely perform its work.
The difference caused when an exact result must be stored as one of the available floating-point values.
An allowed error scaled to the magnitude of the compared values.
Consecutive columns of one row occupy consecutive element positions.
A rule about which addresses are valid starting points for an object type.
A range including its first position but excluding its end position.
An object representing a position that a traversal can examine and advance.
The interval during which a constructed object may be used according to its type’s rules.
Moving responsibility for releasing a resource from one owner to another.
The number of live elements in a container.
The number of elements that fit in currently reserved vector storage without reallocation.
Space that exists but cannot be used for the desired request under an allocator’s rules.
The operation at which a prepared change becomes the visible new state.
An access outside the valid element range of an object.
A program operation for which the C++ standard imposes no behavior requirements.
The registers and other state whose behavior an instruction set promises to software.
The operations and rules a machine exposes to programs.
A named portion of a larger machine register.
Increasing a value’s width by filling the new high bits with zeros.
The address value formed from the components of a machine addressing mode.
A fixed offset included in an address calculation.
The integer result of division after truncation toward zero in this C++ operation.
The part left after multiplying the integer quotient by the divisor.
A rule maintained before every repetition, used to explain the loop’s result.
The order in which a program can execute its operations.
The binary-level agreement for calls, object layout, symbols, and other machine interfaces.
A register whose incoming value a callee must restore when required by the relevant ABI.
Two access paths referring to the same underlying object or storage.
The effects that a valid optimization must preserve under the language’s rules.
A boundary across which code must have different authority to access resources.
Checking that a request satisfies its required shape, range, and permissions before acting on it.
An exception associated with an instruction that could not complete under the current conditions.
The saved execution position used to retry an operation after a recoverable condition is repaired.
Eligible to receive CPU time, though not necessarily executing now.
A permitted change from one named state to another after an event.
The mapping context in which a program interprets its virtual addresses.
The underlying storage reached through a mapping or handle.
A fixed-size block in a virtual address space.
A fixed-size physical-memory block that can back a virtual page.
A record containing mapping information and access-control state for a page.
An exception caused when an access violates the mapping’s permission rules.
A cache of recently used virtual-to-physical translations and related access information.
Removing a cached fact when the authoritative state no longer supports it.
Sharing unchanged backing and making a private copy before a permitted private mutation.
Providing backing for a permitted page when an access first requires it.
The elapsed delay for a particular operation or request.
The amount of data that can be transferred per unit time under stated conditions.
Using nearby locations within a short interval.
Using the same location again before its useful cached state is displaced.
The number of entries in one cache set that can hold competing blocks.
The part of a block’s identity used to distinguish blocks selecting the same set.
An access whose required block is already present and usable at the modeled cache level.
A repeated miss caused by restricted placement relative to the chosen fully associative reference model.
The rule selecting which resident item to remove when space is needed.
A cached block containing changes that must be preserved before the block is discarded.
Misses divided by requests reaching a particular cache level.
Average memory-access time calculated under a stated cost model.
A byte position used to locate data in a file.
A division between logical items imposed by a format above the byte stream.
A process-local handle used to request operations on an open resource.
A successful operation that moves fewer bytes than requested.
Temporarily collecting data so it can be passed onward in useful batches.
Requesting that buffered data move to the next layer defined by the API.
A mapping whose writes affect the shared backing according to the mapping API’s rules.
A mapping whose private modifications do not become shared file changes under its contract.
Kernel-maintained state, such as a file offset, that multiple descriptors may reference.
A process-creation operation that creates a child with defined copies and shared references from its parent.
The executable code and associated user-space state installed in a process.
An operation that replaces the calling process’s program image rather than creating a second process.
Collecting a terminated child’s status so its retained process record can be released.
A result describing how a process terminated; its interpretation depends on the termination category.
End of stream: no more bytes will be delivered under the stream’s contract.
A limit that makes a producer wait or reduce output when a downstream consumer cannot keep up.
An asynchronous process notification with delivery and handling rules defined by the OS.
Permitted for use in an asynchronous signal handler under the applicable API’s rules.
A meaningful input unit such as a word or operator produced during parsing.
A validated description of the operations to perform before those operations are started.
One ordering of steps from activities whose lifetimes overlap.
Multiple activities in progress whose steps may be interleaved or run at the same time.
Waiting for a thread’s completion and establishing the completion relationship needed to use its results.
A division of work into ranges or tasks with explicit coverage and overlap rules.
Conflicting concurrent C++ accesses, at least one a write, without the required atomicity or happens-before ordering.
A result that depends on an undesired ordering of otherwise defined operations.
A pair of atomic ordering operations that can establish visibility of preceding work when the acquire observes the release.
An ordering relation used by C++ to determine whether effects are properly ordered between evaluations.
A region whose operations require coordinated access to shared state.
A synchronization object that permits one cooperating owner at a time.
A waiting mechanism used with a mutex and a predicate over shared state.
A return from waiting that does not itself prove the desired condition is true.
Consume already-accepted work before ending a closed queue or stream.
The rules for stopping new work, waking waiters, finishing or discarding old work, and ending lifetimes.
A state in which participants cannot progress because each waits for conditions the waiting participants must supply.
A cycle of waiting dependencies, such as A waiting for B while B waits for A.
Rules that identify application message boundaries within a sequence of bytes.
An ordered sequence of bytes without a promise that transfer calls preserve message boundaries.
A rule deciding whether new work can enter the system given current resource limits.
The chosen behavior when incoming work exceeds capacity, such as rejection, bounded waiting, or dropping.
A notification that an I/O operation may be able to make progress under the API’s conditions.
A nonblocking result indicating that immediate progress is unavailable without waiting.
Completed work divided by the elapsed measurement interval.
A position in an ordered sample or distribution, interpreted using a stated convention.
Doing reusable work once so later operations require less repeated effort.
How a program’s required work or storage grows with input size.
A time-based bound on whole-system speedup when only a stated fraction of work changes.
A resource or phase that limits the performance of the current workload.
A point where data or actions cross between different levels of trust or authority.
The portion of a buffer that the current operation may treat as meaningful input.
A measure that reduces certain consequences or detects certain failures without necessarily preventing the underlying bug.
Using protections with different coverage so one failed assumption does not remove every defense.
A promise that a failed operation leaves the relevant observable state unchanged.
A guarantee about state surviving the failures specified by a storage protocol, distinct from atomic visibility.
A source unit after preprocessing that the compiler processes under the language’s rules.
Combining compiled definitions and resolving references to build a program or library.
The point at which bounded downstream capacity makes an upstream producer wait or reject work.
A rule spanning several components, such as every accepted input producing exactly one recorded result.

2.title: C and C++ for Systems Programming

60.title: From Source Code to Running Program

workshop.problem: A program must print the sum of two readings. Follow the value from a C++ expression to a stream without assuming that one source line equals one CPU instruction.

2.title: C and C++ for Systems Programming

workshop.problem: Change one local copy and one borrowed object. Predict which updates the caller can see.
Bits 4 through 7 hold a four-bit setting. Replace that field in 0xA5 with 3 while preserving every other bit.
An artificial buffer limit is 100 bytes. Each record uses 12 bytes. Reject a request for 9 records without forming an overflowing product.
Model a machine using IEEE 754 binary64 for double. Add one to 2^53 and test whether the stored value changes.
Three int objects form an array. Find the third element and the number of elements between its address and the first.
Sum a bounded range of three integers. The end pointer must stop the loop and must never be read.
Keep a heap-allocated integer alive after a temporary pointer variable leaves its block.
Append three readings and keep their values correct as storage grows. Do not retain a pointer into storage across possible reallocation.
A model arena aligns every allocation to an eight-byte boundary. Allocate requests of 5 and 9 bytes, tracking the consumed space.
A three-element vector has valid indexes 0, 1, and 2. Show the consequence of asking for index 3 using a checked operation.
An abstract machine has a program counter and one accumulator. Execute LOAD 4, ADD 3, then HALT.
Under x86-64 rules, writing EAX clears the upper half of RAX. Contrast this with merely replacing the low 16 bits.
An address model uses base 1000, index 3, scale 4, and displacement 8. Compute the effective address without reading memory.
Divide -17 by 5 and verify how C++17 relates the quotient and remainder.
Sum indexes from zero up to, but excluding, 4. Track the test, body, and increment.
A caller has a saved value of 10 and asks a helper to double 3. The final result must be 16 even if temporary registers are reused.
Two references may name the same integer. Compare updating then reading through the second reference with remembering its old value first.
A kernel-like function must reject a request for more than 8 bytes. The caller cannot bypass the length check in this model.
Model a load that faults because a permitted page is absent. Resolve the page, retry the load, then advance the program counter.
Model process A issuing I/O while process B is ready. A must leave the run queue until its I/O completes.
Two process models both use virtual address 0x1000. Their private maps must hold independent values.
Pages are 4096 bytes. Translate virtual address 0x1234 when virtual page 1 maps to frame 7.
A model page-table entry is present and readable but not writable. Test a read and a write against the same entry.
Model a valid mapping absent from the translation cache while the requested data is already in the data cache.
Two private address-space models initially share a value of 7. A write in the child should leave the parent’s value unchanged.
A link has 10 microseconds of startup latency and transfers 100 bytes per microsecond. Estimate one 100-byte transfer and one 10,000-byte transfer.
Model a 4-by-4 row-major array and a one-line cache whose line holds four elements. Compare row-first and column-first traversal.
A direct-mapped cache has four sets and 16-byte blocks. Decompose addresses 0, 16, and 64.
A cold direct-mapped cache has four lines of 16 bytes. Read addresses 0, 16, 0, 64, 0, 16.
A two-entry cache sees A, B, A, C. Decide which block to evict when C arrives.
A model cache takes 1 ns for the hit lookup. Five percent of accesses incur an additional 40 ns miss penalty.
A file model contains AB followed by CDE. Read three bytes beginning at byte offset 2.
A mock reader returns at most two bytes per call. Copy all five input bytes while keeping a single advancing position.
A model output buffer forwards data after four bytes or an explicit flush. Append AB and CD, then one final E.
Model a file-backed byte sequence. A private view gets its own copy; a shared view refers to the backing bytes.
Model the important fork distinction: ordinary private values are copied, while inherited descriptor references can share one open-file offset.
A state model starts process 42 running shell. A successful exec changes the program image to worker and keeps the process ID.
Model a parent observing a child’s normal exit code 7, then reaping its termination record.
A pipe model begins with two open write endpoints. Closing only one must not cause EOF after its buffered bytes are drained.
A model flag records that attention is needed. Two notifications arriving before the main loop checks the flag can collapse into one pending state.
A tiny shell language accepts words separated by spaces and the pipe symbol |. Tokenize a pipeline before deciding how to launch it.
Use a sequential model of two participants that both read a counter before either writes back its increment. The requirement is to count two events.
Two threads sum disjoint halves of four readings. Each writes a separate result slot; main combines the results only after both joins.
Use atomic accesses but deliberately read twice before storing. Then compare two fetch_add operations.
A producer writes a value, then publishes a ready flag. A consumer must not read the value until it observes readiness.
Two balances total 100. Transfer 10 from one to the other while holding the same lock over both updates.
Model a consumer that arrives after an item was queued and a notification already happened. The queue state must still let it proceed.
Model a queue with capacity two. Reject a third item, consume one, then permit another insertion.
Two transfers need accounts 3 and 8. Sort the lock identities so opposite transfer directions request locks in the same order.
A byte-stream model delivers a length-prefixed message as two fragments. Assemble a complete frame before interpreting it.
A server has 64 MiB reserved for connection state and budgets 2 MiB per admitted connection. Compute the maximum and test the next admission.
Model draining currently available bytes from a nonblocking input. Stop on would-block and keep the partial application message.
Three serial requests take 2, 8, and 5 milliseconds. Compute mean latency and throughput over the 15-millisecond interval.
For the values 2, 4, 6, 8, answer the sum over indexes [1, 4). Precompute prefix sums so repeated range queries need two reads and a subtraction.
Forty percent of a program’s time is in a part you can make twice as fast. Estimate whole-program speedup.
A packet model has an eight-byte header in a ten-byte buffer. It claims five payload bytes; reject the frame without an overflowing addition.
Model a saved guard beside a payload. Detect a changed guard while recognizing that an untouched guard does not prove the payload is valid.
A settings update must preserve the old value if validation fails. Build the candidate separately, and replace the live state only after checking it.

60.title: From Source Code to Running Program

workshop.problem: A complete program adds two parsed constant strings and formats the result. Distinguish source text, compiled operations, live objects, and output bytes.
Sum six readings with two workers. Keep the input alive, give each worker a disjoint output slot, join, and compare with a sequential reference.
